> $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ and $\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$

where $x,$ $y,$ and $r$ are functions of $\theta .$

Using the fact that $r=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we get 

$$
x=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )
$$

and 

$$
y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =6{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we write

$$
y(\theta )=6(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}.
$$

Now, we see that $y(\theta )$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
y=6{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=12u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Finally, we apply the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}\theta } \\  & =12u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

In parts 2 and 3, we found that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Now, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =6\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =3\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /3} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})}{{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{(-3)} \\  & =-\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

Previously, we've found that

$\,$ $\frac{dx}{d\theta }=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,$ and $\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ).$ 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx}) & =\frac{d}{d\theta }(\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta )) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\cdot 2 \\  & =2{sec}^{2}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}{6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{sec}^{3}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Previously, we found that the slope of the tangent line at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}$ is

$$
m=-\sqrt{3}.
$$

The equation of the tangent is

$$
y-{y}_{0}=m(x-{x}_{0}),
$$

where $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ are the coordinates of the point on the curve that correspond to $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Let's work these out. 

In part 1, we found that

$\,$ $x(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,$ and $\,y(\theta )=6{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .$

As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{0} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =3\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}, \\ {y}_{0} & =6{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =6{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =6{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{9}{2}).$ 

Finally, the equation of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{0} & =m(x-{x}_{0}) \\ y-\frac{9}{2} & =-\sqrt{3}(x-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y-\frac{9}{2} & =-\sqrt{3}x+\frac{9}{2} \\ y & =-\sqrt{3}x+9.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The Lagrange error bound states that an upper bound for the error ${R}_{2}$ obtained when using the second-degree Taylor polynomial ${P}_{2}$ about $\theta =a$ to approximate $r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
|{R}_{2}|\le \frac{M}{3!}|\theta -a{|}^{3},
$$

where $M$ is the maximum value of $|{r}^{(3)}(\theta )|$ on the interval between $a=0$ and $\theta =0.2.$

Plugging $\theta =0.2$ and $a=0$ into the above formula gives

$$
\begin{aligned}|{R}_{2}| & \le \frac{M}{6}|0.2{|}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find $M,$ we need to maximize $|{r}^{(3)}(\theta )|$ on the interval $[0,0.2].$ Previously, we found that

$$
{r}^{(3)}(\theta )=-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Notice that for $\theta \in [0,0.2],$ we have

$$
|{r}^{(3)}(\theta )|=|-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta |=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Since $|{r}^{(3)}(\theta )|=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is a decreasing function on the interval $[0,0.2],$ its value is greatest at $\theta =0.$ So,

$$
M=|{r}^{(3)}(0)|=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=6.
$$

Therefore, the upper bound is

$$
\begin{aligned}|{R}_{2}| & \le \frac{6}{6}|0.2{|}^{3} \\  & =(0.2)^{3} \\  & =0.008.\end{aligned}
$$
